title: A man in the land of Uz (Job 1:1–12)
hookLine: a blameless man, and the adversary's question: does he serve for nothing?

lines: A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.
cards: "There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." It opens like a bedtime story: no king's name, no year, no map. The book never says where Uz is.
The man is perfect and upright, the text says, one who feared God and turned away from evil. He has sons and daughters, flocks and herds.
His children take turns throwing feasts in each other's homes, and after every round Job rises early to offer sacrifices for them, in case one of them sinned and cursed God in their heart.
A careful father with nothing to hide. Then the scene changes, and we're not in Uz anymore.

teach.b: We're in heaven, at a gathering before God, and one who comes is called, in Hebrew, ha-satan. The word has "the" in front of it: the adversary, the accuser. He isn't a ruler of his own kingdom here.
He comes with the others and answers to God. God speaks first: "Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth?"

teach.h: DOTH JOB FEAR GOD FOR NOUGHT?
teach.b: And the adversary asks the question the whole book lives inside: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Look at the fence you've put around him, his house, his work, his flocks. Take it away, and he'll curse you to your face.
God allows it: everything Job has is in your hand, but don't touch the man himself. Job knows none of this.

teach.h: WE KNOW WHY. JOB NEVER DOES.
teach.b: That's the strange gift of the book: we know why it's happening, and Job never does. Some readers hear the question turned on themselves. Is goodness a deal?

Am I kind because it works, honest because it pays, faithful because life has gone well? Or is there something underneath that would stay if the rewards stopped? The rabbis didn't agree on who Job was.

teach.h: A REAL MAN, OR A PARABLE?
teach.b: In the Talmud, one teacher says Job never lived at all, that the book is a parable, and others argue for different ages and places. Either way, Uz could be anywhere, and the man could be anyone.

how: Job is one of the books of the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh. Jews study it as a book of wisdom and argument about suffering, and traditional study includes the rabbis' debate over whether Job was a real man or a parable.

games.q: you're the adversary, standing before God. God has just praised Job: none like him in the earth. what do you say?
o: agree that Job is the best man alive.
ask whether Job fears God for nothing.
games.why: "doth Job fear God for nought?" take away the fence around him, he says, and he'll curse you. the whole book lives inside that question.

practice: Pick one good thing you do, calling your mother, honest work, giving, praying, patience with a kid, and ask it quietly: would I still do this if nothing came back?
Don't answer, and don't decide you're a fraud or a saint; let the question sit, unanswered, the way it sits at the start of this book. If you pray, you can bring the question to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: ha-satan, the Hebrew name, with "the" in front of it, for the adversary who comes before God and asks whether Job fears God for nothing. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: for nothing, freely; the word in the adversary's question in Job 1:9.

carryVoice: Your line: is it for nothing. The question stays open, and the whole book lives inside it. Until tomorrow.
